newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hogs seen below year ago, but set to increase.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hogs seen below year ago, but set to increase.

text.p: CHICAGO, Sept 25, Reuter - The number of hogs on U.S. farms is seen holding below year-ago levels for the rest of the year, but supplies may well increase in 1997, livestock market analysts said.
The trend is expected to be confirmed by Friday's quarterly U.S. Agriculture Department Hogs and Pigs Report.

"The report will tell us that we have fewer hogs for the next six months but after that we should start to move toward at least as many or more hogs than we had the previous year," said Chuck Levitt, livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
USDA's data will be released Friday at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT.

Analysts' estimates for all hogs and pigs on U.S. farms as of September 1 averaged 96.2 percent of a year ago and ranged from 95.0 to 97.5 percent. Estimates on hogs kept for breeding averaged 96.8 percent in a range of 94.0 to 99.0 and hogs kept for marketing averaged 96.5 percent of a year ago in a range of 95.0 to 98.0 pct.
Analysts said breeding herd data will be the most scrutinized part of the report. Producers have appeared to be stabilizing the breeding herd recently by sending fewer sows to slaughter.
Dan Vaught, analyst for AG Edwards, said that producers received higher prices for hogs since the last USDA quarterly report, which likely is sparking expansion plans.

"Expanding the breeding herd during the summer is not very hard because the breeding herd is always the largest at the end of June. They only need to retain some gilts and cull fewer sows to increase production," Vaught said.
Cash prices have consistently been over $55 per hundredweight (cwt) and over $60 for a couple of months -- good incentive to expand, Vaught added.
Farrowing intentions were also seen expanding which resulted in some estimates for third quarter farrowings to exceed 100 percent. This will influence hog supplies in the second quarter of 1997.

Levitt noted that it was too late for producers to do anything about hog supplies in the final quarter this year and first quarter next year. However, they could increase production by the second quarter of 1997 which could boost hog supplies to or above the previous year's first quarter. Fourth quarter farrowings were also seen larger which will influence hog supplies next summer.

September-November farrowing intentions estimates averaged 98.7 percent of a year ago in a range of 96.0 to 102.0 percent and December-February intentions projections averaged 99.9 percent in a range of 94.0 to 105.0 percent.
Most analysts also expected the USDA to again make adjustments to previous reports based on slaughter rates not matching previous projections.

"The USDA may have to go back and do some revisions on the June report again because the slaughter numbers haven't matched up well, particularly with the weight breakdown from the last report," Vaught said.

"In June, hog slaughter was way down -- eight to ten percent at times -- and the weight breakdown basically implied a two- to three-percent reduction. Lately slaughter rates have been more than two to three percent below last year when the hog report implied some three to five percent below last year," Vaught added.
